newsitem.title: USA: US House panel chair says welfare rolls plummeting.
newsitem.headline: US House panel chair says welfare rolls plummeting.

text.p: States' welfare caseloads are in "substantial decline," the result not only of a vigorous economy but of congressional pressure on states to reduce welfare rolls, a key U.S. House member said Thursday.
"We have spectacular news," U.S. Rep. Clay Shaw, R-Florida, chairman of the House human resources subcommittee, said at a press briefing.

"The welfare caseload has been declining in almost every state since 1994 and the average rate of decline for 1996 is greater than the decline for 1995," Shaw said in releasing Congressional Research Service figures requested by the subcommittee.
Shaw said the decline "seems to be picking up steam."
Forty states out of 50 have experienced a 10-percent decline since 1994. Twenty-two of those states had declines of 15 percent or more.

The results were more dramatic when the research service calculated declines starting in the months when states' caseloads were at their highest, Shaw said. Instead of an average 10-percent caseload decline, the figure jumped to 17 percent, he said.

Offering examples, Shaw said caseloads between September 1995 and September 1996 dropped 28.4 percent in Wisconsin, 28.1 percent in Maryland, 22.7 percent in Oregon, 17.5 percent in Oklahoma, 17.2 percent in Nevada, 13.8 percent in Montana and Kansas, 13.6 percent in Massachusetts and 12.3 percent in Indiana.
